headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and cascading errors; Goose’s filesystem/MCP/tooling can steer Airflow workflows if outputs are reused without verification.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airflow has no direct shared channel with Goose, but Goose can read/write the user filesystem and use MCP, while Airflow can egress broadly. If Goose’s outputs are copied into Airflow DAGs, configs, or task inputs, attacker-controlled content can be treated as instructions. The pathway is plausible but not default without a bridge.
conditions: IF Goose writes content into a shared workspace that Airflow later ingests
IF an operator copies Goose-generated text into Airflow DAGs or task parameters
mitigations: Separate Airflow DAG repos from Goose working directories
Require manual review of any Goose-generated config before deployment
Disable or restrict MCP servers used by Goose
Use a read-only handoff folder for artifacts
Add a lint step that rejects instruction-like text in DAG inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches files in the cwd and user filesystem, and Airflow has broad network egress plus API calls. If the pair shares a workspace, Goose can expose file contents that Airflow then moves into external systems or logs. Airflow itself does not show secret handling here, so the main risk is workspace-mediated leakage rather than guaranteed exfiltration.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory tree
IF Airflow tasks transmit Goose-produced files or logs to external services
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared cwd
Mount Goose on a separate workspace from Airflow
Redact secrets before Airflow reads any Goose output
Turn off verbose task logging for shared artifacts
Use per-agent service accounts and separate storage buckets

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose can write the filesystem and modify git state, and its concurrency model explicitly shares state via filesystem. Airflow’s profile does not show write isolation or locking, so if both touch the same repo or working tree, concurrent edits and git mutations can collide. Uncertainty about Airflow’s locking pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF Airflow and Goose write to the same repository or working directory
IF Airflow tasks mutate git state without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories per agent
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Make Airflow outputs append-only where possible
Run Goose in a branch-specific checkout
Add a pre-commit check that rejects concurrent workspace mutation

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can act on files and shell commands, while Airflow is a data orchestrator that can consume generated artifacts. If Goose-produced outputs are treated as authoritative by Airflow DAGs or downstream tasks, a bad fact or malformed file can cascade into automated actions. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, so the safer high severity applies.
conditions: IF Airflow tasks consume Goose-generated artifacts without validation
IF Goose output is used to parameterize automated jobs or shell steps
mitigations: Insert schema validation between Goose and Airflow
Require human approval for Goose-generated DAG changes
Use checksum or signature checks on transferred artifacts
Limit Airflow tasks to read-only inspection of Goose output
Add a canary run before any production DAG update

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for Airflow versus Goose in the provided profiles. Goose handles model-provider and extension tokens, while Airflow’s profile shows no sensitive data classes or compliance constraints. The only plausible issue is operator-managed policy mismatch, which is not enough for medium.
conditions: IF the operator routes regulated data through Goose extensions or Airflow tasks
IF local retention or residency policies are imposed outside these profiles
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces
Document retention rules for any shared artifacts
Review extension tokens before enabling new integrations
Keep compliance-sensitive jobs on separate infrastructure
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention
